newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU has wide powers in competition field.
newsitem.headline: EU has wide powers in competition field.

text.p: The European Union's 1990 merger regulation gives the European Commission sweeping powers to review corporate mergers and to demand changes or even ban them if it finds they would damage competition.

The regulation gives the EU executive the right to vet mergers with a combined worldwide turnover of at least five billion European currency units ($5.45 billion) where each firm has an EU turnover of 250 million Ecus or more.
The firms do not need to be based in the 15-nation bloc.
However, the merger must have an impact on several EU markets. The regulation does not apply if each of the firms concerned achieves two-thirds of its turnover within a sole member state.
The merger regulation introduced a "one-stop shop" for the review of corporate link-ups, replacing a system where companies had to notify a deal to several national competition agencies.
The regulation gives the EU executive one month to either clear a deal or launch a second-phase four-month investigation.

It states that a deal which creates or strengthens a dominant position "as a result of which effective competition would be significantly impeded in the common market or in a substantial part of it shall be declared incompatible with the common market."

If a merger goes ahead anyway, the Commission may impose fines of up to 10 percent of the companies' turnover, the amount reflecting the "nature and gravity of the infringement". The Commission has not yet had to impose fines in any merger cases.
